sentences.text: Last, the extra signals for fishing vessels working close together.
In the International rules they’re in Annex two.
In the Inland rules they now sit inside Rule twenty-six itself.
They’re optional, they’re carried lower than the main fishing lights, and they’re visible at least a mile.
The exam asks you to match each signal to its meaning, so let’s go down the table.
A trawler shooting her nets, putting them out: two white lights in a vertical line.
A trawler hauling her nets, bringing them in: white over red.
A trawler whose net has come fast on an obstruction: two red lights in a vertical line.
Two reds usually means trouble, and here the trouble is a snagged net.
Vessels pair trawling may each aim a searchlight forward and toward the other boat of the pair.
And a purse seiner hampered by her gear may show two yellow lights in a vertical line, flashing alternately.
Sail: sidelights and sternlight, no masthead light, and red over green if she likes.
Next time, the vessels at the top of the ladder, and the lights of boats at anchor and aground.
